lessons.title: GOSUB and RETURN
intro: Sometimes the same few lines are needed in several places. Instead of copying them, you write them once as a subroutine and call it with GOSUB.
GOSUB 100 works like GOTO 100, but BASIC remembers where it came from. When the subroutine reaches RETURN, the program jumps back to the line right after the GOSUB.
Subroutines usually sit at the end of the program. Put a STOP before them, so the main program doesn't accidentally run into them.

exercises.explanation: Line 10 jumps into the subroutine first and prints A. RETURN brings the program back to line 20, which prints B.

exercises.prompt: Call the subroutine that starts at line 200.
exercises.explanation: GOSUB jumps to the subroutine and remembers where to come back. GOTO would never come back.

options: To the line right after the GOSUB that called it
To the first line of the program
To the line right after RETURN
exercises.explanation: BASIC remembers each GOSUB. RETURN goes back to the line that follows it, so the main program continues where it left off.

exercises.prompt: This program prints HELLO, DONE, HELLO and then stops with ?RETURN WITHOUT GOSUB. After which line is a STOP missing?
exercises.explanation: After line 20, the program simply continues with line 100 and runs into the subroutine a second time. A STOP after line 20 prevents that.

exercises.prompt: How often does this program print HI?
exercises.explanation: Every GOSUB runs the subroutine once. Three GOSUBs, three HIs, and the PRINT line was only written once.

exercises.prompt: Build a program that prints HI twice using one subroutine.
exercises.explanation: The main program calls the subroutine twice, then STOP keeps it from running into the subroutine a third time.

lessons.title: Subroutines with Values
intro: A subroutine can use every variable of the program. That's how you hand it values: set a variable, then GOSUB.
The subroutine can also leave a result in a variable, which the main program then uses after the RETURN.
Careful: because all variables are shared, a subroutine can accidentally change a variable the main program still needs, like a loop counter.

exercises.explanation: The subroutine reads X (4) and leaves the result 8 in Y. After RETURN, line 30 prints it.

exercises.prompt: Which variables can a subroutine use?
options: Only variables created inside the subroutine
None, it needs its own copies
exercises.explanation: In Dartmouth BASIC, all variables are shared. The subroutine sees and changes the same variables as the main program.

exercises.prompt: End the subroutine so the program goes back.
exercises.explanation: Every subroutine ends with RETURN. END or STOP would stop the whole program.

exercises.prompt: A subroutine can call another one. What does this print?
exercises.explanation: The first subroutine prints A and calls the second, which prints B. Each RETURN goes back one step, until line 20 prints C.

exercises.prompt: This should print three lines, but it prints only one. Which line causes it?
exercises.explanation: The subroutine changes I, which is also the loop counter. After NEXT I, I is already 6 and the loop ends. Use a different variable in the subroutine.

exercises.prompt: Build a program that hands 7 to a subroutine, which doubles it, and prints 14.
exercises.explanation: Set X, call the subroutine, and print the result it left in Y.

lessons.title: Organizing with Subroutines
intro: Bigger programs stay readable when they're split into parts. The main program at the top only calls subroutines, like a table of contents.
A common habit is to start subroutines at round numbers like 1000, 2000 and 3000, each with a REM line saying what it does. That leaves plenty of room for new lines.
A subroutine can contain loops and IFs too. Anything that would otherwise be copied is a good candidate.

exercises.prompt: Why do programmers often start subroutines at numbers like 1000?
options: It keeps them apart from the main program and leaves room for new lines
exercises.explanation: It's a habit, not a rule. Big gaps make the program easier to read and to extend.

exercises.prompt: Add a note that explains what the subroutine does.
exercises.explanation: A REM line at the start of each subroutine works like a heading.
The subroutine prints N stars and then ends the line. First N is 3, then 2.

exercises.prompt: Why does this program never print DONE?
options: The subroutine has no RETURN, so it runs straight into END
STOP in line 30 runs too early
PRINT can't be used in a subroutine
exercises.explanation: Without RETURN, the program never goes back to line 20. It continues to line 110 and ends.

exercises.prompt: Which part of a program is the best candidate for a subroutine?
options: Lines that are needed in several places
A single LET that runs once
exercises.explanation: Subroutines pay off when the same work is needed more than once. Write it once, call it everywhere.

exercises.prompt: Build a program that prints HELLO between two lines of stars.
exercises.explanation: The star line is written once in the subroutine and called before and after HELLO.
